item.title: Grand loop: existence of the highest weight crystal bases $(\mathcal L(\lambda),\mathcal B(\lambda))$
item.statement:
Let $\lambda\in P^+$ and let $V(\lambda)=L(\lambda)$ be the simple integrable highest weight module with highest weight vector $v_\lambda$ ([[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]]). Let $\mathcal L(\lambda),\mathcal B(\lambda),\mathcal L(\infty),\mathcal B(\infty)$ be the lattices and bases of [[def-kashiwara-lattices-lambda-and-infinity]], let $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ be the Kashiwara operators, let $\pi_\lambda:U_q^-\to V(\lambda)$, $\pi_\lambda(P)=Pv_\lambda$, and let $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu},\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}$ be the tensor maps of [[lem-highest-weight-tensor-maps-and-their-adjunction]]. For $\alpha=\sum_in_i\alpha_i\in Q_+$ write $|\alpha|:=\sum_in_i$ and $Q_+(r):=\{\alpha\in Q_+:\ |\alpha|\le r\}$.

(i) For every integer $r\ge0$ the following interlocking statements are all true.
- A(r): $\tilde e_i\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}\subseteq\mathcal L(\lambda)$ for all $i\in I$ and $\alpha\in Q_+(r)$.
- B(r): $\tilde e_i\mathcal B(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}\subseteq\mathcal B(\lambda)\cup\{0\}$ for all $i$ and $\alpha\in Q_+(r)$.
- C(r): for all $i$, $\alpha\in Q_+(r)$, $b\in\mathcal B(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha+\alpha_i}$ and $b'\in\mathcal B(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}$, one has $\tilde f_ib=b'$ if and only if $b=\tilde e_ib'$.
- D(r): for all $\alpha\in Q_+(r)$, $\mathcal B(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}$ is a $\mathbb Q$-basis of $\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}/q\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}$.
- E(r): for all $\lambda,\mu\in P^+$ and $\alpha\in Q_+(r)$, $\Phi_{\lambda,\mu}\bigl(\mathcal L(\lambda+\mu)_{\lambda+\mu-\alpha}\bigr)\subseteq\mathcal L(\lambda)\otimes\mathcal L(\mu)$.
- F(r): for all $\lambda,\mu\in P^+$ and $\alpha\in Q_+(r)$, $\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}\bigl((\mathcal L(\lambda)\otimes\mathcal L(\mu))_{\lambda+\mu-\alpha}\bigr)\subseteq\mathcal L(\lambda+\mu)$.
- G(r): $\Psi_{\lambda,\mu}\bigl((\mathcal B(\lambda)\otimes\mathcal B(\mu))_{\lambda+\mu-\alpha}\bigr)\subseteq\mathcal B(\lambda+\mu)\cup\{0\}$ for all $\lambda,\mu$ and $\alpha\in Q_+(r)$.
- H(r): $\tilde e_i\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\alpha}\subseteq\mathcal L(\infty)$ for all $i$ and $\alpha\in Q_+(r)$.
- I(r): $\tilde e_i\mathcal B(\infty)_{-\alpha}\subseteq\mathcal B(\infty)\cup\{0\}$ for all $i$ and $\alpha\in Q_+(r)$.
- J(r): for all $\alpha\in Q_+(r)$ and $b\in\mathcal B(\infty)_{-\alpha}$ with $\tilde e_ib\ne0$, one has $b=\tilde f_i\tilde e_ib$.
- K(r): $\mathcal B(\infty)_{-\alpha}$ is a $\mathbb Q$-basis of $\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\alpha}/q\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\alpha}$ for all $\alpha\in Q_+(r)$.
- L(r): $\pi_\lambda\bigl(\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\alpha}\bigr)=\mathcal L(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}$ for all $\lambda\in P^+$ and $\alpha\in Q_+(r)$.
- M(r): for all $\alpha\in Q_+(r)$, $i\in I$, $\lambda\in P^+$ and $P\in\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\alpha+\alpha_i}$, one has $\tilde f_i(Pv_\lambda)\equiv(\tilde f_iP)v_\lambda\bmod q\mathcal L(\lambda)$.
- N(r): for all $\lambda\in P^+$ and $\alpha\in Q_+(r)$, $\pi_\lambda$ induces a bijection $\{b\in\mathcal B(\infty)_{-\alpha}:\ \pi_\lambda(b)\ne0\}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal B(\lambda)_{\lambda-\alpha}$.
- O(r): for all $\lambda\in P^+$, $\alpha\in Q_+(r)$ and $b\in\mathcal B(\infty)_{-\alpha}$ with $\pi_\lambda(b)\ne0$, one has $\pi_\lambda(\tilde e_ib)=\tilde e_i\pi_\lambda(b)$.

(ii) Consequently $(\mathcal L(\lambda),\mathcal B(\lambda))$ is a crystal basis of $V(\lambda)$ in the sense of [[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]: $\mathcal L(\lambda)$ is a crystal lattice of $V(\lambda)$, $\mathcal B(\lambda)$ is a $\mathbb Q$-basis of $\mathcal L(\lambda)/q\mathcal L(\lambda)$ with $\mathcal B(\lambda)=\bigsqcup_\mu\mathcal B(\lambda)_\mu$, the operators satisfy $\tilde e_i\mathcal B(\lambda)\subseteq\mathcal B(\lambda)\cup\{0\}$ and the partial-inverse axiom, and $\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}V(\lambda)_\mu=\#\mathcal B(\lambda)_\mu$ for all $\mu$. The lattices $\mathcal L(\lambda)_\mu$ and $\mathcal L(\infty)_{-\alpha}$ are free $A_0$-modules.

The proof is the simultaneous root-height induction described below. Work in the finite-support auxiliary regular datum before choosing fundamental or arbitrarily large dominant weights, then transport the chosen label grading back. No global Z[q,q^-1]-freeness or global basis is a premise. Choice is inherited only from the generic/classical component-rank supplier underlying the field negative-half form; choosing a basis in one finite-dimensional weight space and taking its field dual require no further AC. The field-dual lattice is defined before any self-duality conclusion.
item.strategy:
Run the complete real-root specialization of JKK §7 in source dependency order, with every auxiliary argument proved locally. First use the finite-support regularization supplier: a finite coordinate summand contains the finitely many original top labels and all simple roots. Its auxiliary primitive-coroot perfect datum has integral fundamental weights, independent simple roots, the same d_i and Cartan matrix, and K_i=K_(d_i H_i). It identifies the graded support categories and all operations here; auxiliary fundamental/large weights may be used in the proof, with the final assertions restricted to the original labels. No embedding of the old torus algebra is asserted.
0. Heights0 and1: check the top and F_i position using the finite module endpoints and the infinite negative-half identity; if lambda(h_i)=0 the module's lowering position is zero. Obtain all A–O directly. Field spanning of both recursively defined lattices follows independently by induction on root degree: U^-[-alpha]=Σ_i F_i U^-[-alpha+alpha_i], and V(lambda)_(lambda−alpha)=Σ_i F_i V(lambda)_(lambda−alpha+alpha_i). On a homogeneous element its i-string components have smaller degrees; F_i acts on position n as [n+1]_i times the next f̃_i position. Thus the recursive lowering words span over Q(q). This gives rational lattices in every finite-dimensional component; finite generation and torsionfreeness imply A0 freeness because A0 is an actual DVR.
1. Assume all A–O below r. The finite string-component argument (JKK7.3–7.4) applies ẽ_i to a finite decomposition, inducts on its largest position, and subtracts the lower terms, proving each top component lies in the lattice. For a residue basis word, B/C below r give exactly one nonzero string component modulo q. The same proof uses H/I/J below r in U^-. Apply the proved rank-one tensor supplier to these top components: it gives tensor-lattice stability, the f̃ comparison phi(first)>epsilon(second), the ẽ comparison phi(first)≥epsilon(second), and partial inverses wherever both factor degrees are below r. In particular, a nonconstant word with a last color change i_t≠i_(t+1)=...=i_r splits on v_(Lambda_i_t)⊗v_mu into one tensor residue with both factor heights strictly between0 and r (JKK7.7): the final repeated color lowers the second factor because Lambda_i_t pairs0 with that different coroot, and the first occurrence of i_t lowers the first factor. At the color change, E_(i_t) kills the repeated different-color tail and F_(i_t) sends it exactly to F_(i_t)v_(Lambda_i_t)⊗tail + q_(i_t)v_(Lambda_i_t)⊗F_(i_t)tail. The second term is in q times the tensor lattice; all remaining prefix inputs have both heights below r, so the rank-one tensor rule controls them. The tensor-lattice decomposition into Σ_i f̃_i of height r−1 plus v_lambda⊗L(mu) at height r is JKK7.8: apply all raising operators to a tensor residue; if each kills it the first factor must be top, otherwise take its predecessor using the lower-height partial-inverse rule. Interior b⊗b′ with both heights below r has such a predecessor unless its first factor is top. For the remaining first-boundary L(lambda)[degree alpha]⊗v_mu, a generating nonzero word is congruent to the same word applied to v_lambda⊗v_mu: at each prefix use the top-second tensor rule, with only the previous degree involved. If the first word vanishes modulo q it contributes only qL. The first-boundary contribution is therefore also in the lowering-image span plus qL. The second-boundary contribution is exactly the explicit v_lambda⊗L(mu) remainder. Nakayama now upgrades the resulting finite generated residue span to lattice equality, without needing a basis in either boundary component at height r. These arguments use neither F(r) nor a basis at height r.
2. E(r): recursively span by f̃_i of height r−1 and apply Phi, which commutes with module Kashiwara operators. Tensor stability on the lower inputs gives the image inclusion. Keep general F(r),G(r) until the final steps; they are not yet available.
3. Large-weight microlocal calculation (JKK7.10–7.11): on the n-th string position, q_i^-1 K_i E_i has the rank-one coefficient q_i^(a−2n+1)[a−n+1]_i. Its inverse has nonnegative q-valuation when the position is admissible. If q_i^-1K_iE_i u is in q^N L, string-component extraction therefore puts all positive top components in q^N L. Choosing N above the finitely many negative valuations of the relevant divided-power multiplications makes f̃_i^m u congruent to F_i^(m)u, and ẽ_iF_i^(m)u congruent to F_i^(m−1)u whenever the top is long enough. For P=F_i^(n)Q with e_i'Q=0, the exact identity q_i^-1K_iE_i(Qv_lambda)=−(1−q_i²)^-1 q_i^(2<h_i,lambda+alpha_i+wt Q>)(e_i''Q)v_lambda makes these errors arbitrarily high-valuation when all lambda(h_j) are large. Fixed finite-degree words make the bounds uniform. Thus both operators commute with pi_lambda modulo q in large weights. To prove M(r) for arbitrary lambda, add a sufficiently large mu, apply Phi_(lambda,mu), use E(r−1), lower-height projection and the tensor rule, then apply the second-top map S, whose f̃ compatibility modulo q follows by checking its top-second and positive-second string positions. This is JKK7.9/7.12 and uses only S's U^--linearity. Iterate M(r) on a finite word to obtain pi(L∞)⊂Llambda and equality of word residues. Recursive spanning then gives Llambda=pi(L∞)+q Llambda; its finitely generated quotient vanishes by Nakayama, proving L(r). If every lambda(h_i) exceeds the coefficient of alpha_i, the field Serre ideal Σ_iU^-F_i^(lambda(h_i)+1) has no component in degree alpha. Hence pi is a field isomorphism there, and L(r) makes it a lattice isomorphism. No global integral basis is needed.
4. A(r),H(r), with the actual valuation-improvement argument of JKK7.15–7.17. Choose a common pole bound N for ẽ_i on the finite set of original lambda, relevant fundamental weights, and U^- component. At large mu the large-weight isomorphism/previous-degree bounds give the same bound. The tensor component of total degree alpha also has ẽ_i pole bound N: interior factor degrees are below r and already integral; at boundary degrees extract positive string components in q^-N and use the rank-one tensor lattice. If N>0, a pure-color word is checked exactly by rank one. Every other word splits at its last color change on a fundamental weight and a large complementary weight, into an interior tensor residue plus q times the bounded tensor lattice. Raising therefore improves the bound to q^(-N+1); applying Psi in raised degree uses F(r−1), not F(r). For an original or fundamental top tau, compare the word on v_tau⊗v_mu with its first-factor word⊗v_mu if the latter is nonzero; Phi in raised degree uses E(r−1), and extracting the second top improves its bound by the same one power. If the original word is already in qL, the improvement is immediate. Transfer to U^- by its large-weight lattice isomorphism and microlocal congruence. Thus N decreases by1 simultaneously, terminates at0, and proves A/H. The string-component/tensor-lattice arguments now apply at r (JKK7.20).
5. I(r): use the same interior tensor splitting of a nonpure word, apply the tensor raising rule and lower B/G, then transport through large-weight pi. The pure-color case is rank one. For O(r), take a surviving word residue in V(lambda); on tensoring with a large second top its word has residue u⊗v_mu. Raising on such a top-second tensor is congruent to ẽ_i u⊗v_mu by the rank-one rule. Compare with the large-weight negative-half raising calculation, apply Phi and then S, giving O(r). I, O and the already proved residue image statement give B(r). This is JKK7.21–7.24, with no same-height C or F premise.
6. Establish the module lattice pairing before J(r), following JKK7.25. String extraction is now justified by A(r). Homogeneous top string components of different positions are orthogonal: repeated contravariance reduces their pairing to a highest vector paired with a positive F_i-power, which is zero. At equal position n with top rank-one weight a, the exact norm factor is q_i^(n(a−n))[a choose n]_i∈1+qA0. For a positive-height word pair, recursively write one input as f̃_i of a lower-height input, extract both strings, and apply these unit norm ratios. This gives B_lambda(Llambda,Llambda)⊂A0 and B_lambda(f̃_i u,v)≡B_lambda(u,ẽ_i v) modulo q. At n=0 or a=0 the endpoint terms are zero, so no finite-string identity is misused.
7. Derive the full degree/color large-weight pairing normalization; do not cite the incorrect printed direction in JKK7.26. If Q has degree−nu and P=F_iR, the exact commutator gives
B_lambda(F_iR v,Qv)=(1−q_i²)^-1[B_lambda(Rv,(e_i'Q)v)−q_i^(2<h_i,lambda−nu+alpha_i>)B_lambda(Rv,(e_i''Q)v)].
Induct on height with B_infty(F_iR,Q)=B_infty(R,e_i'Q). For nu=Σ_i n_i alpha_i, the constant term is C_nu B_infty(P,Q), C_nu=∏_i(1−q_i²)^(-n_i)∈1+qA0, in the module pairing, so B_lambda(Pv,Qv)≡C_nu B_infty(P,Q) to any prescribed q-order once every lambda(h_i) is large. The other term at each induction stage carries a large positive power of q_i, and its remaining lower-degree pairing is a finite polynomial in the variables q_j^(2lambda(h_j)) with coefficients in Q(q); its valuation is bounded below uniformly on large dominant labels. Thus the error can be made uniformly arbitrarily small for the finitely many vectors of any component. This proves the general formula, not just a rank-one diagnostic. Kashiwara91 Lemma4.7.1 has the consistent constant term; JKK7.26's stated factor is reversed relative to its displayed recurrence.
8. Field-dual lattice transfer and special F(r). Choose an A0 basis P_k of L∞[-nu] and its field dual Q_j under the nondegenerate field form, B_infty(P_k,Q_j)=delta_kj. Define L∞^vee=Σ_j A0Q_j; Q_j need not lie in L∞. The corrected comparison gives B_lambda(P_kv,Q_jv)≡delta_kj modq, because C_nu≡1. The pairing matrix is therefore invertible over A0, and the large-weight field/lattice isomorphism gives pi_lambda(L∞^vee)=Llambda^vee and (Llambda^vee)^vee=Llambda. This is dual-lattice equality from an invertible pairing matrix, not self-duality. For mu large, decompose the tensor lattice as in step1. The lowering-image part goes through Psi by F(r−1). Pair the remainder v_lambda⊗Lmu with every u∈L_(lambda+mu)^vee; write u=Pv_(lambda+mu), P∈L∞^vee by the just-proved transfer. In ΔP only the extreme K_nu⊗P can pair with a first top. Its scalar is q^(Σ_i n_i d_i lambda(h_i))∈A0, and Pv_mu∈Lmu^vee. Adjointness therefore places Psi of that remainder in the double-dual L_(lambda+mu). This proves special F(r) for large mu (JKK7.28) without assuming unimodularity.
9. J(r): for a nonpure lowering word use its fundamental/large-weight interior tensor residue, whose two factor heights are <r. If its raised negative-half residue is nonzero, large-weight raising compatibility and lower G make the tensor raised residue nonzero. The lower tensor partial inverse then gives b_tensor=f̃_i ẽ_i b_tensor. Apply Psi to this degree-r congruence using special F(r) from step8, then use large-weight pi's lattice isomorphism and operator congruences to obtain b=f̃_i ẽ_i b. The pure-color word uses the exact infinite string identity. This is the full JKK7.29 seam and uses no same-height self-duality, general F or N.
10. C(r) follows for a surviving module edge by string extraction and, for its converse, by lifting via L/O and using J. To prove D/K, take a finite relation among basis-word residues and apply each ẽ_i. Below r the raised residues form an independent basis; the partial-inverse statement makes the surviving preimages under each ẽ_i distinct. Every positive-degree word residue has a nonzero raising edge: in V it is an f̃_i predecessor and the string-component argument gives the inverse; in U^- use ẽ_i f̃_i=id on its actual lattice. Hence every relation coefficient vanishes. Recursive definitions give spanning. N(r) is residue surjectivity plus injectivity: if two surviving preimages agree, raise by an i that does not kill their common module image, use O and lower N, then J to conclude equality.
11. General F(r) and G(r) last. Once D/K and the partial inverse are proved, a residue killed by all ẽ_i in positive height is zero, by independence of the raised predecessor residues. For a field vector whose raisings all lie in the lattice, take its minimal q-pole N; if N>0, its normalized nonzero residue is killed by all raisings, a contradiction. Apply this to Psi of an arbitrary tensor lattice element: its raisings lie in L by the tensor stability at r and F(r−1). This proves general F(r). For a tensor basis residue, if every raising vanishes its Psi image vanishes by the same residue detection; otherwise use the tensor partial inverse, lower G and the commutation of Psi with operators to obtain a basis word or zero. Thus G(r) closes the induction. Final module/crystal/lattice/rank assertions follow from A–O, scalar-extension spanning and DVR freeness. No late global Z theorem, QG4 tensor theorem, independent external proof or A0-perfectness premise is used. The inherited choice hypothesis is recorded only from the field half-form supplier; finite dual-basis linear algebra itself is choice-free.

For a residue basis word, B/C below r give exactly one nonzero string component modulo q. The same proof uses H/I/J below r in U^-. Apply the proved rank-one tensor supplier to these top components: it gives tensor-lattice stability, the f̃ comparison phi(first)>epsilon(second), the ẽ comparison phi(first)≥epsilon(second), and partial inverses wherever both factor degrees are below r. In particular, a nonconstant word with a last color change i_t≠i_(t+1)=...=i_r splits on v_(Lambda_i_t)⊗v_mu into one tensor residue with both factor heights strictly between0 and r (JKK7.7): the final repeated color lowers the second factor because Lambda_i_t pairs0 with that different coroot, and the first occurrence of i_t lowers the first factor. At the color change, E_(i_t) kills the repeated different-color tail and F_(i_t) sends it exactly to F_(i_t)v_(Lambda_i_t)⊗tail + q_(i_t)v_(Lambda_i_t)⊗F_(i_t)tail. The second term is in q times the tensor lattice; all remaining prefix inputs have both heights below r, so the rank-one tensor rule controls them. The tensor-lattice decomposition into Σ_i f̃_i of height r−1 plus v_lambda⊗L(mu) at height r is JKK7.8: apply all raising operators to a tensor residue; if each kills it the first factor must be top, otherwise take its predecessor using the lower-height partial-inverse rule. Interior b⊗b′ with both heights below r has such a predecessor unless its first factor is top. For the remaining first-boundary L(lambda)[degree alpha]⊗v_mu, a generating nonzero word is congruent to the same word applied to v_lambda⊗v_mu: at each prefix use the top-second tensor rule, with only the previous degree involved. If the first word vanishes modulo q it contributes only qL. The first-boundary contribution is therefore also in the lowering-image span plus qL. The second-boundary contribution is exactly the explicit v_lambda⊗L(mu) remainder. Nakayama now upgrades the resulting finite generated residue span to lattice equality, without needing a basis in either boundary component at height r. These arguments use neither F(r) nor a basis at height r.
2. E(r): recursively span by f̃_i of height r−1 and apply Phi, which commutes with module Kashiwara operators. Tensor stability on the lower inputs gives the image inclusion. Keep general F(r),G(r) until the final steps; they are not yet available.
3. Large-weight microlocal calculation (JKK7.10–7.11): on the n-th string position, q_i^-1 K_i E_i has the rank-one coefficient q_i^(a−2n+1)[a−n+1]_i. Its inverse has nonnegative q-valuation when the position is admissible. If q_i^-1K_iE_i u is in q^N L, string-component extraction therefore puts all positive top components in q^N L. Choosing N above the finitely many negative valuations of the relevant divided-power multiplications makes f̃_i^m u congruent to F_i^(m)u, and ẽ_iF_i^(m)u congruent to F_i^(m−1)u whenever the top is long enough. For P=F_i^(n)Q with e_i'Q=0, the exact identity q_i^-1K_iE_i(Qv_lambda)=−(1−q_i²)^-1 q_i^(2<h_i,lambda+alpha_i+wt Q>)(e_i''Q)v_lambda makes these errors arbitrarily high-valuation when all lambda(h_j) are large. Fixed finite-degree words make the bounds uniform. Thus both operators commute with pi_lambda modulo q in large weights. To prove M(r) for arbitrary lambda, add a sufficiently large mu, apply Phi_(lambda,mu), use E(r−1), lower-height projection and the tensor rule, then apply the second-top map S, whose f̃ compatibility modulo q follows by checking its top-second and positive-second string positions. This is JKK7.9/7.12 and uses only S's U^--linearity. Iterate M(r) on a finite word to obtain pi(L∞)⊂Llambda and equality of word residues. Recursive spanning then gives Llambda=pi(L∞)+q Llambda; its finitely generated quotient vanishes by Nakayama, proving L(r). If every lambda(h_i) exceeds the coefficient of alpha_i, the field Serre ideal Σ_iU^-F_i^(lambda(h_i)+1) has no component in degree alpha. Hence pi is a field isomorphism there, and L(r) makes it a lattice isomorphism. No global integral basis is needed.
4. A(r),H(r), with the actual valuation-improvement argument of JKK7.15–7.17. Choose a common pole bound N for ẽ_i on the finite set of original lambda, relevant fundamental weights, and U^- component. At large mu the large-weight isomorphism/previous-degree bounds give the same bound. The tensor component of total degree alpha also has ẽ_i pole bound N: interior factor degrees are below r and already integral; at boundary degrees extract positive string components in q^-N and use the rank-one tensor lattice. If N>0, a pure-color word is checked exactly by rank one. Every other word splits at its last color change on a fundamental weight and a large complementary weight, into an interior tensor residue plus q times the bounded tensor lattice. Raising therefore improves the bound to q^(-N+1); applying Psi in raised degree uses F(r−1), not F(r). For an original or fundamental top tau, compare the word on v_tau⊗v_mu with its first-factor word⊗v_mu if the latter is nonzero; Phi in raised degree uses E(r−1), and extracting the second top improves its bound by the same one power. If the original word is already in qL, the improvement is immediate. Transfer to U^- by its large-weight lattice isomorphism and microlocal congruence. Thus N decreases by1 simultaneously, terminates at0, and proves A/H. The string-component/tensor-lattice arguments now apply at r (JKK7.20).
5. I(r): use the same interior tensor splitting of a nonpure word, apply the tensor raising rule and lower B/G, then transport through large-weight pi. The pure-color case is rank one. For O(r), take a surviving word residue in V(lambda); on tensoring with a large second top its word has residue u⊗v_mu. Raising on such a top-second tensor is congruent to ẽ_i u⊗v_mu by the rank-one rule. Compare with the large-weight negative-half raising calculation, apply Phi and then S, giving O(r). I, O and the already proved residue image statement give B(r). This is JKK7.21–7.24, with no same-height C or F premise.
6. Establish the module lattice pairing before J(r), following JKK7.25. String extraction is now justified by A(r). Homogeneous top string components of different positions are orthogonal: repeated contravariance reduces their pairing to a highest vector paired with a positive F_i-power, which is zero. At equal position n with top rank-one weight a, the exact norm factor is q_i^(n(a−n))[a choose n]_i∈1+qA0. For a positive-height word pair, recursively write one input as f̃_i of a lower-height input, extract both strings, and apply these unit norm ratios. This gives B_lambda(Llambda,Llambda)⊂A0 and B_lambda(f̃_i u,v)≡B_lambda(u,ẽ_i v) modulo q. At n=0 or a=0 the endpoint terms are zero, so no finite-string identity is misused.
7. Derive the full degree/color large-weight pairing normalization; do not cite the incorrect printed direction in JKK7.26. If Q has degree−nu and P=F_iR, the exact commutator gives
B_lambda(F_iR v,Qv)=(1−q_i²)^-1[B_lambda(Rv,(e_i'Q)v)−q_i^(2<h_i,lambda−nu+alpha_i>)B_lambda(Rv,(e_i''Q)v)].
Induct on height with B_infty(F_iR,Q)=B_infty(R,e_i'Q). For nu=Σ_i n_i alpha_i, the constant term is C_nu B_infty(P,Q), C_nu=∏_i(1−q_i²)^(-n_i)∈1+qA0, in the module pairing, so B_lambda(Pv,Qv)≡C_nu B_infty(P,Q) to any prescribed q-order once every lambda(h_i) is large. The other term at each induction stage carries a large positive power of q_i, and its remaining lower-degree pairing is a finite polynomial in the variables q_j^(2lambda(h_j)) with coefficients in Q(q); its valuation is bounded below uniformly on large dominant labels. Thus the error can be made uniformly arbitrarily small for the finitely many vectors of any component. This proves the general formula, not just a rank-one diagnostic. Kashiwara91 Lemma4.7.1 has the consistent constant term; JKK7.26's stated factor is reversed relative to its displayed recurrence.
8. Field-dual lattice transfer and special F(r). Choose an A0 basis P_k of L∞[-nu] and its field dual Q_j under the nondegenerate field form, B_infty(P_k,Q_j)=delta_kj. Define L∞^vee=Σ_j A0Q_j; Q_j need not lie in L∞. The corrected comparison gives B_lambda(P_kv,Q_jv)≡delta_kj modq, because C_nu≡1. The pairing matrix is therefore invertible over A0, and the large-weight field/lattice isomorphism gives pi_lambda(L∞^vee)=Llambda^vee and (Llambda^vee)^vee=Llambda. This is dual-lattice equality from an invertible pairing matrix, not self-duality. For mu large, decompose the tensor lattice as in step1. The lowering-image part goes through Psi by F(r−1). Pair the remainder v_lambda⊗Lmu with every u∈L_(lambda+mu)^vee; write u=Pv_(lambda+mu), P∈L∞^vee by the just-proved transfer. In ΔP only the extreme K_nu⊗P can pair with a first top. Its scalar is q^(Σ_i n_i d_i lambda(h_i))∈A0, and Pv_mu∈Lmu^vee. Adjointness therefore places Psi of that remainder in the double-dual L_(lambda+mu). This proves special F(r) for large mu (JKK7.28) without assuming unimodularity.
9. J(r): for a nonpure lowering word use its fundamental/large-weight interior tensor residue, whose two factor heights are <r. If its raised negative-half residue is nonzero, large-weight raising compatibility and lower G make the tensor raised residue nonzero. The lower tensor partial inverse then gives b_tensor=f̃_i ẽ_i b_tensor. Apply Psi to this degree-r congruence using special F(r) from step8, then use large-weight pi's lattice isomorphism and operator congruences to obtain b=f̃_i ẽ_i b. The pure-color word uses the exact infinite string identity. This is the full JKK7.29 seam and uses no same-height self-duality, general F or N.
10. C(r) follows for a surviving module edge by string extraction and, for its converse, by lifting via L/O and using J. To prove D/K, take a finite relation among basis-word residues and apply each ẽ_i. Below r the raised residues form an independent basis; the partial-inverse statement makes the surviving preimages under each ẽ_i distinct. Every positive-degree word residue has a nonzero raising edge: in V it is an f̃_i predecessor and the string-component argument gives the inverse; in U^- use ẽ_i f̃_i=id on its actual lattice. Hence every relation coefficient vanishes. Recursive definitions give spanning. N(r) is residue surjectivity plus injectivity: if two surviving preimages agree, raise by an i that does not kill their common module image, use O and lower N, then J to conclude equality.

For a field vector whose raisings all lie in the lattice, take its minimal q-pole N; if N>0, its normalized nonzero residue is killed by all raisings, a contradiction. Apply this to Psi of an arbitrary tensor lattice element: its raisings lie in L by the tensor stability at r and F(r−1). This proves general F(r). For a tensor basis residue, if every raising vanishes its Psi image vanishes by the same residue detection; otherwise use the tensor partial inverse, lower G and the commutation of Psi with operators to obtain a basis word or zero. Thus G(r) closes the induction. Final module/crystal/lattice/rank assertions follow from A–O, scalar-extension spanning and DVR freeness. No late global Z theorem, QG4 tensor theorem, independent external proof or A0-perfectness premise is used. The inherited choice hypothesis is recorded only from the field half-form supplier; finite dual-basis linear algebra itself is choice-free.

item.title: The residue translation functors give the integrable Fock-space action
item.statement: Assume AC. The exact residue functors on genuine finite-n parabolic blocks have multiplicity-free generalized-standard flags given by valid single-entry moves $i\to i+1$ and $i+1\to i$. Their K0 operators are the full integrable $gl_{I^+}$ Fock Chevalley action, satisfying the integral Chevalley/Serre relations on the standard basis. For each simple, a residue translate vanishes exactly when its corresponding crystal edge is absent; otherwise it is a self-dual indecomposable with simple equal head/socle $L(\tilde f_iA)$ or $L(\tilde e_iA)$. The full tensor Fock module is represented by all standard classes; the ground-state class, with $M(A_\Lambda)=L(A_\Lambda)=P(A_\Lambda)$, generates only its multiplicity-one highest constituent. No action on labels alone proves the K0 relations or head/socle statement.
item.strategy: The earlier Casimir supplier proves actual flags, the standard-class isomorphism, relations and local integrability BEFORE the head lemma, so there is no circular dependence on this combined theorem. The local affine-Hecke helper proves the complete categorical extremal-string/simple-socle argument and matches labels by the actually read source-upper Chevalley leading-term proof. Apply it with E=f_i,F=e_i (and the swapped root orientation), then use restricted duality. For the ground multiset the column-strict admitted label is unique: successive strict entries at least their row ground values, with that minimal total weight forcing equality. The15 highest-weight/character bases therefore make its standard simple and projective. All quantum global/form claims have their own explicit later dictionary; this is the ungraded categorical result.

item.title: Bar invariance and the congruence modulo $q$ do not imply balancedness
item.statement:
Bar-fixedness and a prescribed residue alone do not imply balancedness, global parametrization or uniqueness. First, in the two-dimensional sl2 module use L′=A0(v+w)⊕qA0v and its ACTUAL bar lattice A∞(v+w)⊕q^-1A∞v. With V_A=Av⊕Aw, its balanced part is Z(v+w), whose residue image misses the valid nonzero class qv+qL′. The vector v+w is bar fixed but L′ fails the crystal-lattice weight/stability axioms; it is a general-lattice failure of existence/parametrization, not by itself a uniqueness counterexample.
For a genuine separate nonuniqueness witness use the one-dimensional trivial module Q(q)v with integral lattice Av, bar v=v, and crystal lattice L″=q^-1A0v (all operators0) with bar L″=qA∞v. Its balanced intersection is Zq^-1v⊕Zv⊕Zqv, mapping onto the Z-residue generator q^-1v+qL″ with nonzero kernel. The two DISTINCT bar-fixed integral vectors (q+q^-1)v and(q+q^-1)v+v have the same nonzero crystal residue. Thus even a valid scaled crystal lattice plus bar invariance/congruence does not force unique global lifts without the actual balanced map. Neither example is the canonical top-normalized Kashiwara triple of a highest module.
item.strategy:
For L′ use a=v+w,t=v. Its integral zero intersection is Z[q]a⊕qZ[q]t; its infinity intersection is Z[q^-1]a⊕q^-1Z[q^-1]t, because bar sends qv toq^-1v. The triple intersection is Za, while the integral zero residue is Za⊕Zqv. This proves the missing qv class; v itself is not in L′, so v+qL′ is undefined and never asserted. The elementary ẽa=v and coefficient calculation show the lattice is free/full but not crystal stable or weight decomposed, distinguishing this failure from the next example.
In the trivial module all Kashiwara operators vanish; every homogeneous full free scaled A0 lattice is a genuine crystal lattice, and q^-1v is its residue basis representative. The simultaneous Laurent coefficient bounds for L″ and bar L″ are exponents−1≤k≤1, giving exactly the displayed rank3 Z intersection. Reducing modulo qL″=A0v kills v and qv but not q^-1v. Both proposed integral vectors are fixed by q↦q^-1, lie in the simultaneous intersection and have coefficient1 on q^-1v, hence the same nonzero crystal class; their difference v≠0 is in the kernel. This proves the promised nonuniqueness directly. The canonical globalization theorem requires its exact integral balanced map, not merely a crystal lattice, and remains unchanged.

item.title: Changing the equality case in the tensor rule breaks the partial-inverse axiom
item.statement:
Claim refuted: on the product of two crystals the two operators may be defined by the same kind of comparison, namely
$$\tilde f_i^{\prime}(b_1\otimes b_2)=\tilde f_ib_1\otimes b_2\ \text{ if }\ \varphi_i(b_1)\ge\varepsilon_i(b_2),\qquad \tilde e_i^{\prime}(b_1\otimes b_2)=\tilde e_ib_1\otimes b_2\ \text{ if }\ \varphi_i(b_1)>\varepsilon_i(b_2),$$
with the second factor used in the remaining cases and $0$ whenever the selected factor maps to $0$; that is, the two equality cases of [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]] are exchanged.

Counterexample: take $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2$, the rank-one simples of highest weights $a=b=2$ with divided bases $v_j=F_1^{(j)}v_0,\ w_k=F_1^{(k)}w_0$, and the vertex $b=v_1\otimes w_1$. Then $\varphi_1(v_1)=1=\varepsilon_1(w_1)$, so the modified rule uses the non-strict comparison and acts on the first factor: $\tilde f_1^{\prime}(v_1\otimes w_1)=v_2\otimes w_1$. At the image $b'=v_2\otimes w_1$ one has $\varphi_1(v_2)=0\le\varepsilon_1(w_1)=1$, and the modified $\tilde e_1^{\prime}$ acts on the first factor only when $\varphi_1>\varepsilon_1$, so it acts on the second factor: $\tilde e_1^{\prime}(v_2\otimes w_1)=v_2\otimes w_0\ne v_1\otimes w_1$. Hence $\tilde f_1^{\prime}b=b'$ while $\tilde e_1^{\prime}b'\ne b$: the partial-inverse axiom fails, so $(B(a)\otimes B(b),\tilde e^{\prime},\tilde f^{\prime})$ is not a crystal, and a fortiori not the crystal $B(a)\otimes B(b)$ of [[thm-crystal-basis-tensor-product-rule]]. The same failure occurs if one uses the strict comparison for both operators, or the non-strict comparison for both; by contrast the rank-one computation of [[lem-rank-one-tensor-strings-have-the-crystal-limit-rule]] shows that with the convention of [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]] the string through $v_0\otimes w_1$ is $v_0\otimes w_1,v_1\otimes w_1,v_1\otimes w_2$ of length three, whereas the modified rule produces the four-element chain $v_0\otimes w_1,v_1\otimes w_1,v_2\otimes w_1,v_2\otimes w_2$, so the modified graph has the wrong component size and cannot be the crystal of $V(2)\otimes V(2)=V(4)\oplus V(2)\oplus V(0)$.
item.strategy:
A finite computation at the boundary case $\varphi_i(b_1)=\varepsilon_i(b_2)$, following the rank-one analysis of [[lem-rank-one-tensor-strings-have-the-crystal-limit-rule]].

1.1 Set $a=b=2$ and index the divided bases by their string positions, so that $\varphi_1(v_j)=2-j=\varepsilon_1(v_j)$ reversed: $\varepsilon_1(v_j)=j$ and $\varphi_1(v_j)=2-j$, and similarly for $w_k$. The vertex $v_1\otimes w_1$ satisfies $\varphi_1(v_1)=1=\varepsilon_1(w_1)=1$; this is the equality case in which the two conventions differ. [given, algebra]

2.1 Under the modified rule $\tilde f_1^{\prime}$ acts on the first factor at this vertex, because it uses $\varphi_1\ge\varepsilon_1$: $\tilde f_1^{\prime}(v_1\otimes w_1)=v_2\otimes w_1$. [step 1.1]

2.2 At $v_2\otimes w_1$ one has $\varphi_1(v_2)=0$ and $\varepsilon_1(w_1)=1$, so both the modified and the original rule select a factor by the comparison of $0$ with $1$; the modified $\tilde e_1^{\prime}$ acts on the first factor only when $\varphi_1>\varepsilon_1$, which fails, so it acts on the second: $\tilde e_1^{\prime}(v_2\otimes w_1)=v_2\otimes w_0$. [step 2.1, algebra]

3.1 Therefore $\tilde e_1^{\prime}\tilde f_1^{\prime}(v_1\otimes w_1)=v_2\otimes w_0\ne v_1\otimes w_1$, contradicting the partial-inverse axiom of [[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]] that every crystal satisfies, so the modified data is not a crystal; the same computation with both comparisons strict fails at $\varphi_1=\varepsilon_1+1$, and with both non-strict at a vertex with $\varphi_1=\varepsilon_1$. [step 2.2, step 1.1]

4.1 Compare component sizes: the original rank-one tensor rule of [[lem-rank-one-tensor-strings-have-the-crystal-limit-rule]] gives $\tilde f_1(v_j\otimes w_k)=v_{j+1}\otimes w_k$ if $2-j>k$ and $v_j\otimes w_{k+1}$ otherwise; through $v_0\otimes w_1$ this is $v_0\otimes w_1\to v_1\otimes w_1\to v_1\otimes w_2$, a chain of three, which is $B(2)$ in the component decomposition of $V(2)\otimes V(2)=V(4)\oplus V(2)\oplus V(0)$. The modified rule instead produces $v_0\otimes w_1\to v_1\otimes w_1\to v_2\otimes w_1\to v_2\otimes w_2\to0$, a chain of four, which is not a component of the crystal of any module in the decomposition. [step 3.1, given]

5.1 Consequently the equality case in [[def-tensor-product-of-crystals]] is not a matter of taste: the assignment $\tilde f_i$ strict and $\tilde e_i$ non-strict is the one for which the partial-inverse axiom and the component sizes of the rank-one computation agree, and the alternative conventions produce different coloured graphs with a different number of vertices in the affected string. [step 3.1, step 4.1] ∎

item.title: The full Fock space is not automatically the irreducible basic module
item.axiom_use: Inherits the axiom of choice through [[thm-restricted-partition-component-is-the-basic-crystal-in-the-symmetric-group-convention]]; the exhibited non-containment facts themselves are finite checks.
item.statement: At e3 the entire F_sym is strictly larger than its cyclic basic module. The shape4 is not3-restricted since4−0≥3; its conjugate is1111 (NOT111), which is not3-regular since part1 has multiplicity4≥3. Both raw M4 in F_sym and |1111> in F_QG are nonzero and are OUTSIDE their respective field basic modules, and their ambient lower global lifts are outside too. The full signature rule remains meaningful on these shapes in the full Fock crystal; for example restricted-model e0(4)=3 is an edge of another component, not a route into the empty component. Modular/basic signature statements restricted to restricted labels do not apply to4 as a basic label.
item.strategy: Restricted/regular and transposed size checks are immediate. To prove actual vector exclusion rather than graph-only exclusion, apply the actual top-isotypic crystal-lattice splitting theorem to F_QG at its maximal one-dimensional top Lambda0: F0_QG∩V(Lambda0) is the canonical lower lattice and its residue basis exactly the regular empty component. If raw1111 were in this module, its nonzero nonregular residue would lie in that component's span, contradicting residue-basis splitting. Its ambient lower lift has the same residue and is also excluded. Transport by the genuine field and chart isomorphism J gives M4 and its lift. At4, the sole removable0 node is(1,4), so the full restricted signature yields e0→3; neither shape is in the restricted empty component (3−0≥3), hence this edge is compatible with the full decomposable crystal. This corrects the native assertion that the signature had no ambient crystal meaning, while preserving the modular restricted-vertex hypothesis and the strongest field-vector boundary.

item.title: The whole partition Fock space is not the basic representation
item.statement: For every finite e≥2, the entire partition Fock module F is strictly larger than M=U_q|empty>=V(Lambda0). The raw basis vector |1^e> is not in M, and its ambient lower lift G(1^e) is also not in M. The full field decomposition is ⊕_(k≥0) V(Lambda0−k delta)^(⊕p(k)); the Λ0 multiplicity is1, and higher constituents are nonzero. Thus the full crystal has all partitions, its empty component exactly e-regular partitions, and the nonregular ambient lower vectors do not form the basis of that single highest module.
item.strategy: The full crystal and decomposition theorem already proves all labels/counts, preserving the approved p(k) claim. To prove the stronger RAW-vector exclusion do not use graph membership alone. Lambda0 is a maximal weight with one-dimensional top, so the actual top-isotypic splitting theorem for crystal lattices gives F0∩M=canonical L(Lambda0), and its residue basis is exactly the empty component. If |1^e> were in M it would lie in this intersection; its nonzero residue in F0/qF0 is the nonregular shape1^e, contradicting residue-basis splitting. The same proof applies to G(1^e), which is congruent to that shape moduloqF0. Directly its part1 occurs e times, so it is not e-regular. Freeness/nonzero residue is provided by the normal basis, and saturation of the A0 intersection comes from the proved lattice splitting, not a global Laurent integral decomposition.

item.title: Good and cogood nodes by residue-signature reduction
item.statement: For an i-node word in the fixed INCREASING-content order write+=(addable),−=(removable), cancel adjacent−+ until no such pair remains. Surviving minuses are normal REMOVABLE nodes and the FIRST surviving minus is the good node for e_i; surviving pluses are conormal ADDABLE nodes and the LAST surviving plus is the cogood node for f_i. Missing chosen sign means the operator is0. Equivalently read DECREASING content/columns (top-to-bottom), cancel+−, take good=LAST− and cogood=FIRST+. These name conventions match the usual Fayers good deletion/cogood addition. They are combinatorial string data, not a selection by minimum ordinary Chevalley exponent.
item.strategy: Unique reduction follows by the stack matching of−+; any two local deletions commute or share no cancellable pair, so the matching survivors do not depend on deletion order. Reverse the word to obtain+− with first/last exchanged. The fixed-residue cube supplies the actual operator interpretation and both endpoints; no existence/module assertion is needed in this Definition. At e3 lambda2,i2 the two pluses choose the top-right cell(1,3), not the native leftmost opening at(2,1). At lambda21,i2 the minus-plus pair cancels; F2|21> may be nonzero but tilde f2 is0. This explicitly refutes the native minimizer shortcut.

item.title: The integral residue lattices $L_A(\infty)$ and $L_A(\lambda)$
item.statement:
Let A=Z[q,q^-1], with rational DVRs A0 atq=0 and A∞ atq=∞. Put M_A=U_A^- or V_A(lambda)=U_A^-v_lambda, L=L∞ or Llambda, and L^-=bar L. The integral residue lattice is L_Z=M_A∩L, a Z[q]-module, and its bar lattice is L_Z^-=M_A∩L^-, a Z[q^-1]-module. Its balanced intersection E_Z=M_A∩L∩L^- is a Z-module. Since q^-1M_A=M_A, M_A∩qL=qL_Z; consequently the residue map L_Z/qL_Z→L/qL is injective and is Z-linear. Its image is an integral subgroup of the rational crystal space, not the entire Q-space. No Laurent-A-linearity is asserted on the residue lattice or map.
The field projection pi_lambda restricts to an A-linear surjection U_A^-→V_A(lambda) and sends L_Z(infinity) into L_Z(lambda), by the already proved grand-loop lattice projection. The module V_A is U_A-stable: reordering reduces actions on v_lambda to negative divided powers and toral Gaussian scalars in A, with all positive generators killing the top except the unit. No global freeness, residue spanning or balancedness is assumed here. The integral residue subgroup for the negative half is proved below to be ZB∞; the module subgroup ZBλ is a consequence of globalization.
item.strategy: Intersections inherit Z[q] or Z[q^-1] actions because these rings preserve the corresponding rational DVR lattices and the Laurent integral module. They do not inherit q^-1 or q actions on the wrong chart. If x∈M_A∩qL, then q^-1x∈M_A∩L, proving the exact quotient kernel. Pi preserves both the integral form by definition and the rational crystal lattice by the completed grand loop, so it preserves the intersection. Reordering and the integral highest character prove V_A stability, using actual A Gaussian scalars rather than the false equality U_A^0v=Q(q)v. These are definitions and already-proved supplier consequences, independent of global integral bases.

item.title: The bar lattice and the divided-power integral lattice of a based module
item.statement:
Fix $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]\subseteq\mathbb Q(q)$ and the crystal limiting ring $A_0\subseteq\mathbb Q(q)$ of [[def-the-local-ring-at-q-zero]], and put $A_\infty:=\psi(A_0)$, the image of $A_0$ under the semilinear involution $\psi(q)=q^{-1}$, i.e. the ring of rational functions regular at $q=\infty$; $A_0$ and $A_\infty$ are the rational local rings at0 and infinity; the integral affine chart coordinate rings are Z[q] and Z[q^-1].

Let $M$ be one of $U_q^-$ or $V(\lambda)=L(\lambda)$ ($\lambda\in P^+$). Equip $M$ with the bar involution $\psi$ of [[lem-the-lusztig-integral-form-is-stable-under-bar-and-contravariant-duality]]: on $U_q^-$ the semilinear algebra involution $\psi(q)=q^{-1}$, $\psi(E_i)=E_i$, $\psi(F_i)=F_i$, $\psi(K_h)=K_h^{-1}$; on $V(\lambda)$ the induced semilinear involution determined by $Pv_\lambda\mapsto\psi(P)v_\lambda$ (well defined because the highest vector is fixed). Let $M_A\subseteq M$ be the divided-power integral form: $M_A=U_A^-$ for $M=U_q^-$, and $M_A=V_A(\lambda):=U_A^-v_\lambda$ for $M=V(\lambda)$ ([[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]]; $U_A^-$ and $V_A(\lambda)$ are $\psi$-stable). Let $L$ be the Kashiwara crystal lattice of $M$ over $A_0$: $L=L(\infty)$ for $U_q^-$ and $L=L(\lambda)$ for $V(\lambda)$ ([[def-kashiwara-lattices-lambda-and-infinity]], [[thm-grand-loop-existence-of-highest-weight-crystal-bases]]).

Define the **bar lattice** $L^-:=\psi(L)$, an $A_\infty$-submodule of $M$, and the **balanced part** $E:=M_A\cap L\cap L^-$. The definition keeps three structures on the same $\mathbb Q(q)$-vector space strictly separate: the $A$-module $M_A$, which is not assumed free and not claimed to be contained in $L$; the free $A_0$-module $L$; and the free $A_\infty$-module $L^-$. No equality $L^-=L$, no inclusion $M_A\subseteq L$, no freeness of $M_A$ and no identification $E=M_A$ are asserted; freeness is a conclusion of the balanced-triple construction, whereas E is a Z-module of global lifts and is not equal to the Laurent lattice M_A. The bar lattice is not the form-dual (upper) lattice, which is defined later on this page. Intersections M_A∩L and M_A∩L^- are respectively Z[q]- and Z[q^-1]-modules, generally not A-modules. The balanced part E is a Z-module; its Laurent extension A⊗_Z E is the full integral module once globalization is proved. More generally a based integrable module (M,B) here means exactly: B is a homogeneous field basis; M_A=⊕_b A b is U_A-stable; the semilinear involution fixing B is U/bar compatible; and L0=⊕_b A0 b with residue B is a crystal local basis at0. These are Lusztig27.1.2(a)–(d) after v=q^-1 and the integrable Bao–Wang extension. Such data do not automatically imply integral Θ action on an arbitrary based pair. A based subobject is a U-submodule spanned by a subset of B; a based quotient is its quotient with the complementary basis images. Based morphisms send B to the target basis or0 and have kernels spanned by the killed basis subset. These exact integral/bar-compatible maps, not arbitrary field summands, are used in tensor inheritance.
item.strategy: A definition fixing the three lattices. The involution $q\mapsto q^{-1}$ maps $A_0$ isomorphically onto $A_\infty$, so $\psi(L)$ is an $A_\infty$-lattice generating $M$. $\psi(M_A)=M_A$ holds on $U_A$ by [[lem-the-lusztig-integral-form-is-stable-under-bar-and-contravariant-duality]], and $V_A(\lambda)$ is $\psi$-stable because $\psi(F_{i_1}^{(r_1)}\cdots F_{i_k}^{(r_k)}v_\lambda)=F_{i_1}^{(r_1)}\cdots F_{i_k}^{(r_k)}v_\lambda$ on divided-power monomials. Nothing is asserted about $M_A\cap L$; in particular the definition hides no integral-freeness assumption and no self-duality of the lower lattice. No choice principle is used. The general four based conditions are checked independently; the associated bar fixes a field basis but U compatibility and U_A stability are real requirements. Basis-subset subobjects give saturated free integral sublattices and free complementary quotients. Their bars are the restrictions/quotients of the ambient bar, and their crystal local data are inherited because their subset/kernel is closed under the module action and the residue operators. This is the actual source27.1.3–27.1.4 interface, not an assumed integral splitting of a semisimple field module.

item.title: The Fock-space convention dictionary for finite type-A quantum modules
item.statement: Use source parameter $s$ and library parameter $t=s^{-1}$. For every finite interval $[k,r]\subset I^+$ choose the type-A root datum with full $gl$ coordinate weight lattice, including its central torus. The source generators have $D_av_b=s^{\delta_{ab}}v_b$, $E_av_b=\delta_{a+1,b}v_a$, $F_av_b=\delta_{a,b}v_{a+1}$ and coproduct $\Delta E_a=1\otimes E_a+E_a\otimes D_aD_{a+1}^{-1}$, $\Delta F_a=F_a\otimes1+D_a^{-1}D_{a+1}\otimes F_a$. The semilinear Hopf dictionary sends library $E_a,F_a$ to these same divided generators and $K_h$ to $D_{-h}$; the library parameter $t$ maps to $s^{-1}$. Thus root-label weights are preserved, while toral numerical eigenvalues use the reciprocal parameter. Bar sends $s\mapsto s^{-1}$, fixes $E,F$ and inverts $D$. The natural highest weight is $\delta_k$, its dual highest weight is $-\delta_r$, and the fundamental wedge weight is $\delta_k+\cdots+\delta_m$. Every fundamental factor has its own highest-vector-normalized bar, integral lattice and divided-string crystal charts. Infinite intervals are defined by compatible finite intervals below. The SOURCE Fock $L,T,P$ families and the library form-dual upper family will be compared through their actual forms, not identified by their names.
item.strategy: Check toral actions, commutator and Serre relations generator by generator after t=s^-1 and K_h→D_-h. Both numerator and denominator of the E/F commutator change sign, so E,F are unchanged. The library coproduct E→1⊗E+E⊗K_i^-1 and F→F⊗1+K_i⊗F becomes the displayed source coproduct. Divided quantum integers are invariant under reciprocal parameter. The full coordinate lattice supplies the gl centre, so neither delta_k nor−delta_r is mislabelled as a semisimple fundamental weight. Fundamental wedges are constructed next; their internal antisymembedding is primitive integral but is not claimed lower-q0 based. Apply actual8 between these independently based fundamental factors on finite intervals; infinite-rank/tail compatibility is proved locally.

item.title: Dual crystals reverse arrows and weights: two small computations
item.statement:
The example computes the dual crystal of [[prop-dual-crystal-and-reversal-conventions]] in two small cases.

(A) For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2$, let $B(1)=\{v_0\xrightarrow{1}v_1\}$ with $wt(v_0)=\lambda_1,\ wt(v_1)=-\lambda_1$ and $\varepsilon_1(v_0)=0,\varphi_1(v_0)=1,\varepsilon_1(v_1)=1,\varphi_1(v_1)=0$ (as in [[ex-tensor-crystal-b-one-tensor-b-one-for-sl-two]]). Then $B(1)^\vee=\{v_0^\vee,v_1^\vee\}$ has the single arrow $v_1^\vee\xrightarrow{1}v_0^\vee$, weights $wt(v_0^\vee)=-\lambda_1,\ wt(v_1^\vee)=\lambda_1$, and $(\varepsilon_1,\varphi_1)$ equal to $(1,0)$ at $v_0^\vee$ and $(0,1)$ at $v_1^\vee$. Hence $B(1)^\vee\cong B(1)$ as crystals, realized with the highest vertex $v_1^\vee$.

(B) For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_3$, let $B(\lambda_1)=\{u_1\xrightarrow{1}u_2\xrightarrow{2}u_3\}$ be the standard crystal of [[ex-highest-components-in-a-small-type-a-two-tensor-crystal]]. Then $B(\lambda_1)^\vee=\{u_1^\vee,u_2^\vee,u_3^\vee\}$ has the arrows $u_2^\vee\xrightarrow{1}u_1^\vee$ and $u_3^\vee\xrightarrow{2}u_2^\vee$, weights $-\lambda_1,\ -\lambda_2+\lambda_1,\ \lambda_2$ at $u_1^\vee,u_2^\vee,u_3^\vee$, and $\varepsilon/\varphi$ exchanged; this is the crystal $B(\lambda_2)$ of the dual three-dimensional module, so $B(\lambda_1)^\vee\cong B(\lambda_2)$.

(C) On the tensor square of (A), $(B(1)\otimes B(1))^\vee\cong B(1)^\vee\otimes B(1)^\vee$ under $(b_1\otimes b_2)^\vee\mapsto b_2^\vee\otimes b_1^\vee$; both sides split as $B(2)\sqcup B(0)$ because each of $B(2),B(0)$ is self-dual along the chain reversal (weights $2\lambda_1,0,-2\lambda_1$ are symmetric).

item.title: Canonical elementary crystal extraction and highest-weight survivors
item.statement: For every real symmetrizable Cartan datum, the canonical negative-half crystal has strict elementary embeddings Psi_i(b)=bar b tensor b_i(-c_i(b)), where c_i(b)=epsilon_i(star b), bar b=(e_i^star)^c_i(b)b, c_i(bar b)=0, and every nonvacuum vertex has positive extraction for some i. The negative-half reversal star permutes B(infinity) without signs; this unsigned conclusion is proved from the existing signed lattice theorem and positive highest-weight tensor residues, not assumed. The survivors of pi_lambda are exactly c_i(b)<=lambda_i for all i; with weight lambda+wt(b), inherited raising and surviving lowering, and epsilon/phi, they are B(lambda). Any two lowering-generated, everywhere-lowerable negative crystals with strict nonpositive elementary extractions and positive extraction at every nonvacuum vertex are uniquely isomorphic by their lowering words; the proof uses finite color cycles and terminates after a height bound. Consequently for any field and any general homogeneous nondegenerate Q of the first two lemmas, the shift-orbit simple-module crystal is canonically B(infinity), its first-strand cyclotomic simple graph is B(lambda), and the graph labeled by indecomposable projective COVERS P(S) is the same graph under the unscaled cover–simple pairing. Projective crystal operators here mean operators transported on cover labels; no arbitrary #-dual-of-simple identification, generic global-basis theorem, or independent linear Kashiwara action on the projective class basis is asserted.
item.strategy:
## Right strings and the adapted survivor criterion, initially with signs

Define the right string operators by star conjugating the left normalized Kashiwara operators. Because star is an isometry of the actual crystal lattice and signed crystal set, every positive crystal residue b lies in exactly one right-string position c_i(b)>=0. On a lattice lift u one has

    u=sum_(n>=0) u_n F_i^(n),   u_n in ker(star e_i' star),

with every u_n in the crystal lattice, and modulo q only the component n=c_i(b) is nonzero. Its top coefficient has residue ±bar b for some positive crystal residue bar b with c_i(bar b)=0. For the negative half the lattice-component argument is proved directly by the same finite tail calculation as the module string lemma: if u=sum_n F_i^(n)v_n, set T_n=e-tilde_i^n u; then v_n=T_n-f-tilde_i T_(n+1) lies in the lattice. Induction on the largest position, using the residue partial inverse, shows that a basis residue has exactly one nonzero component and that its top residue is positive. Root height makes the tails finite. This proves the half version without applying an integrable-module-only Statement to U^-. Conjugating this argument through the signed lattice theorem gives the asserted signed right version, without assuming unsigned star. The integer c_i(b) is epsilon_i of the absolute value of star b.

The field right ideal U^- F_i^t is the direct sum of right-string positions n>=t. Its adapted global subset is therefore precisely the positive indices b with c_i(b)>=t: conjugate the already proved left-string adapted global subset through star, whose possible signs do not affect which A-basis vectors span the ideal. The based quotient's field kernel is the sum of these right ideals at t=lambda_i+1. Since all are adapted to ONE global basis, their sum is the span of the union of their basis subsets. Therefore

    pi_lambda(b)!=0 iff c_i(b)<=lambda_i for every i.    (A)

This proves the highest-weight survivor criterion already with signed star. It neither assumes unsigned star nor infers an adapted intersection from an arbitrary linear sum. The surviving residues are bijective with B(lambda) by the existing based quotient/grand loop. Raising cannot turn a survivor into a killed nonzero residue: if e_i b were killed, the ALL-residue lowering identity pi_lambda(f_i(e_i b))=f_i pi_lambda(e_i b)=0 and the negative-half partial inverse f_i e_i b=b would force b killed, a contradiction. Thus every nonzero raising iterate of a survivor survives. Combining this with the surviving-residue raising identity proves equality of the entire raising lengths, epsilon_i(pi_lambda b)=epsilon_i(b), including the zero endpoint. This supplies the precise statistic identification used later in the finite-model construction without circularly using elementary embeddings. Raising on survivors and surviving lowering are exactly these existing projection compatibilities. The shifted statistics are epsilon_i(b) and epsilon_i(b)+<h_i,lambda+wt(b)> because B(lambda) is the actual highest-weight module crystal; raising preservation gives epsilon equality, and its rank-one formula gives phi.

## Canonical elementary embedding by finite highest-weight tensor models

Fix color i and a finite set of lowering words of height at most H. Work in the regularized finite support. Choose lambda_i=0 and lambda_j large for j!=i, large enough that no right ideal for those j meets any relevant root component of height at most H+1. Choose N>H+1. The total label lambda+N Lambda_i is then large at every relevant color, so its projection identifies the canonical B(infinity) vertices and all edges under consideration with the corresponding finite-degree vertices of B(lambda+N Lambda_i). Apply the strict highest-weight tensor embedding into B(lambda) tensor B(N Lambda_i).

Throughout these finite lowering paths the second factor is a pure i-string f_i^m u_(N Lambda_i). Indeed initially it is highest. For j!=i its epsilon_j is0 at every pure i-string position: E_j commutes with F_i and kills the highest vector, so all such vectors are E_j-highest. The first factor's phi_j is positive and larger than any second epsilon_j in the bounded degree, because lambda_j is chosen large. Thus both lowering and raising of any j!=i act on the first factor. Color i preserves the pure i-string form. Its string endpoint N is not reached in this height bound.

Lift the first residue b_1 uniquely to its surviving positive residue b' in B(infinity). Replace the second pure i-position m by b_i(-m) in the elementary crystal. The finite tensor rules become exactly those on B(infinity) tensor B_i: for i, lambda_i=0 means the first phi_i is epsilon_i(b')+<h_i,wt(b')>, and the second epsilon_i is m. For j!=i the elementary statistics are -infinity, so its tensor rule selects the first factor, just as the large-lambda finite model does. The finite tensor epsilon formula reduces to epsilon_j(b') for j!=i because lambda_j is large; for i it reduces to max(epsilon_i(b'),m-<h_i,wt(b')>). Root weights add to wt(b')-m alpha_i. Thus the replacement preserves the generic weight, epsilon and formal phi statistics as well as every considered operator.

This construction is independent of lambda,N WITHOUT assuming a stabilization theorem. Define its candidate value on a lowering word w by computing w(u_infinity tensor b_i(0)) using the actual generic tensor rules. The preceding finite-model argument shows that this computation agrees with the replacement of the finite tensor image for every bounded path. If two words w,w' give the same b in B(infinity), choose one common finite bound and one common pair lambda,N. Their images in B(lambda+N Lambda_i) coincide, hence their strict tensor images coincide, and the unique surviving lifts of their first factors coincide. Therefore the candidate generic tensor values coincide. Conversely if the candidate values coincide, choose the same finite model for the two words; its first-factor projections and second positions coincide, and injectivity of Phi followed by the large-label projection identification gives w u_infinity=w' u_infinity. This proves a well-defined injective Psi_i, independent of all choices.

For lowering use the same finite model on a word and that word with one appended operator. For raising use a model containing the vertex, its raising neighbor if nonzero, and the next boundary; strictness of finite Phi and the already checked branch/statistic formulas give Psi_i(e_j b)=e_j Psi_i(b), including zero. Hence

    Psi_i:B(infinity)->B(infinity) tensor B_i

is strict, sends the vacuum to u_infinity tensor b_i(0), and every elementary coordinate is nonpositive. This is an actual finite-word construction, rather than a citation to Kashiwara Theorem8.2.

## Identifying the elementary coordinate with the right-string index

The remaining coordinate identification can be checked on the coproduct rather than assumed from unsigned star. For a homogeneous P of root beta, the coefficient of one i in the second tensor factor of Delta(P), after extracting its toral K_i, is e_i''(P). On homogeneous root beta this derivative is

    e_i''(P)=q_i^(<h_i,beta>-2) (star e_i' star)(P).

Check this first on a generator. Both sides then satisfy the same twisted deletion rule, with prefix versus suffix twists interchanged; the displayed homogeneous scalar converts one rule into the other. Hence their kernels agree. Coassociativity or repeated deletion shows that every higher pure-second-i coefficient is a nonzero field scalar multiple of the corresponding repeated derivative; it therefore vanishes on P in the right-string kernel. Thus projecting Delta(P) onto the terms with pure i root degree in the second factor leaves exactly P tensor1.

Apply this to the right expansion u=sum_n u_n F_i^(n) above, acting on v_lambda tensor v_(N Lambda_i) with lambda_i=0. Every mixed-color second-factor term has a different second root degree and is removed by the pure-i projection. For u_n in the right kernel only u_n tensor1 survives that projection. In Delta F_i^(n), every term whose first divided power F_i^(a) has a>0 kills v_lambda before u_n acts. The remaining term is K_i^n tensor F_i^(n), and K_i^n v_lambda=v_lambda because lambda_i=0. Therefore the exact pure-second-i projection is

    sum_n pi_lambda(u_n) tensor F_i^(n)v_(N Lambda_i).   (B)

No uncontrolled q shift occurs in this formula with the actual native coproduct. The derivative equality above is only used to identify the kernel; scalar rescalings do not change it.

The coefficient u_c, c=c_i(b), has signed positive crystal residue ±bar b with right index0. Its projection at lambda_i=0 survives by (A); all other coordinates survive because lambda_j is large. Thus its projected residue is nonzero. Every n!=c coefficient has zero crystal residue. Formula (B) consequently has exactly one nonzero pure-i tensor residue, at position c. On the other hand Phi(pi_(lambda+N Lambda_i)b) is a positive pure-i tensor residue by the finite model. It follows that its elementary coordinate m is exactly c_i(b), and that the top right-string coefficient u_c has POSITIVE residue bar b, not negative. Thus

    Psi_i(b)=bar b tensor b_i(-c_i(b)),
    c_i(bar b)=0,  b=(f_i^right)^(c_i(b)) bar b.          (C)

In particular every nonvacuum b has positive extraction at some i: star b is a signed nonvacuum crystal residue, and the canonical lowering-generated crystal has a nonzero raising direction on its absolute value.

## Unsigned star follows rather than being assumed

Induct on root height. The vacuum is fixed by star. For a positive-height b choose i with c_i(b)>0. Formula (C) gives b=(f_i^right)^c bar b with bar b a POSITIVE residue of strictly smaller height. Apply star:

    star b=f_i^c(star bar b).

By induction star bar b is positive, and canonical lowering preserves positive crystal residues. Therefore star b is positive. Since star is an involution, it permutes B(infinity) bijectively without signs. This proves unsigned star for every real symmetrizable datum from the actual signed theorem plus tensor positivity. Then c_i(b)=epsilon_i(star b) is the usual epsilon_i^star, and (C) is the exact canonical elementary extraction formula. The proof does not invoke a symmetric-type geometric basis.

## Identification of the generic and cyclotomic module crystals

the preceding local one-step and jump/embedding lemmas construct the generic module strict elementary embeddings, with extraction coordinate epsilon_i^L and positive extraction on every nonvacuum module. Both its graph and the canonical graph just constructed are generated by lowering words from their vacua and have every lowering operator nonzero. The finite-extraction comparison lemma proved next identifies the two graphs uniquely by lowering words. Strictness also forces their elementary extraction coordinates to agree: the comparison tensor identity holds on the vacuum and on every lowering word, so

    epsilon_i^L(M)=epsilon_i^star(b_M).

The local one-step lemma's first-dot criterion identifies the cyclotomic module vertices with epsilon_i^star(b_M)<=lambda_i. Equation (A) identifies exactly that subset with the surviving canonical vertices, hence with B(lambda). Existing projection compatibility proves the raising and surviving-lowering correspondence, while The local jump lemma's actual normal-length formula gives the canonical epsilon/phi data. This proves the full all-field/general homogeneous-Q simple crystal theorem, using exactly the stated local quantum and algebra suppliers. Projective vertices are labeled by the indecomposable projective COVER P(M) of each simple M. The cover–simple Hom pairing transports this graph: E/F crystal labels on covers mean P(e-tilde M), P(f-tilde M), with zero when the simple label is zero. This does not identify P(M) with an arbitrary # dual of M. Independently defined projective Kashiwara operators still require their exact leading-term convention.

## Finite-extraction comparison proof

There is a smaller recognition contract for this application, whose proof is elementary. Suppose C and D are crystals, each generated from its unique weight-zero vertex by lowering words, every f_i is everywhere nonzero, and each has strict elementary embeddings Psi_i with nonpositive elementary coordinates and a positive coordinate for some i on every nonvacuum vertex. Assume the weight support of a vertex is finite and extraction subtracts a nonnegative multiple of alpha_i from its root weight. Then there is a unique crystal isomorphism C=D carrying the two vacua to each other.

Proof. Fix a finite color set containing the support of a lowering word. Cycle through these colors, applying Psi_i to the current first factor, and leave every elementary tensor factor already extracted in place. Tensoring a strict embedding with identity maps is strict: for each color the tensor max formulas preserve epsilon/phi and weight, hence preserve the branch inequality including equality. Therefore every finite composite is strict and injective. Each extraction lowers the nonnegative height of the first factor by its elementary coordinate c. If an entire cycle makes no extraction from a nonvacuum factor, that factor is unchanged throughout the cycle, yet its support has a color with positive extraction, contradiction. Thus after at most the starting height many cycles (and one harmless final cycle) the first factor is the vacuum. Extraction of absent colors is zero: a nonzero alpha_i extraction would give a residual root weight with negative alpha_i coefficient, forbidden. Consequently this finite procedure works in both crystals using the same finite color cycle.

For a word w of length h, use h+1 cycles. Every prefix has height at most h, so both images of every prefix have vacuum first factor. Strictness computes the image of w by applying that same lowering word to the same tensor of a vacuum and elementary zero vertices. While the underlying vacua belong to different crystals, their weights and epsilon/phi are identical and their raising operators vanish; at each intermediate prefix the first factor is still the vacuum, so a nonzero lowering operation cannot take place in that first factor. All operations occur in the identical elementary factors, and the resulting elementary coordinates are identical. If two words w,w' produce the same vertex in C, use a common finite color set and enough cycles for both lengths; their identical C images give identical coordinate tensors, hence identical D images and, by injectivity, identical D vertices. Interchanging C and D gives the converse. Mapping a lowering word in C to that word in D is therefore a well-defined bijection. It preserves lowering by construction, raising by partial inverses, weights by word content, and epsilon/phi because the common strict finite tensor embeddings preserve these statistics. Uniqueness follows from lowering generation. This proves the lemma.
